name: Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain
role: Union Army officer, governor of Maine (1867–1871) and president of Bowdoin College
summary: Chamberlain defended the Union and backed constitutional Reconstruction to secure citizenship rights after emancipation. As governor he advocated tax-supported education, public support for rail development and continued state authority over railroads. During Maine’s disputed 1879 election he kept the peace until the courts could resolve the contest.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: His centennial address named the division of labor as one of the benefits of diversified local production and credited it with contributing to Maine’s prosperity.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: His centennial address praised freehold tenure and held up small independent landowners as a safeguard against the social damage he attributed to concentrated estates.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: He urged ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment, which guaranteed citizenship to persons born in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction.

consent-of-governed.rationale: He placed the ultimate authority of American government in the people of the United States and grounded the Union’s permanence in that authority.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: He urged Maine to ratify the Fourteenth Amendment as a step toward securing the citizenship rights won through emancipation and criticized the amendment for leaving room for racial exclusion.

country-wealth-only-from-land.rationale: His centennial address attributed Maine’s potential prosperity to skilled manufacturing and the processing of raw materials as well as to farming and natural resources.

death-penalty.rationale: As governor he ordered the execution of Clifton Harris in an aggravated murder case and commuted two other death sentences to life imprisonment.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: His first address called for the citizenship rights secured through the war to be put into law and criticized the proposed Fourteenth Amendment for leaving room for legal disabilities based on race.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: He volunteered for the Union Army and commanded Union troops in the campaign that defeated the Confederacy and ended its attempt to leave the United States.

government-encourage-intercultural-conta.rationale: In his official report on the Paris exposition he praised international exhibitions for letting nations learn from one another’s work and softening competition through the exchange of ideas.

head-commands-forces.rationale: In reorganizing the Maine militia he kept the new companies independent of a regimental command and directly responsible to the commander-in-chief, the governor.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: His centennial address advocated diversified manufacturing and argued that technical skill and productive machinery could improve working life and general prosperity.

member-state-blocks-federal-overreach.rationale: In his postwar speech he said Congress was the judge of its own national powers, while state governments retained authority within their own sphere.

more-religion-public.rationale: He described churches and schools as sources of New England’s social prosperity and called sustaining religious institutions and practices a duty owed to society.

night-watchman-state.rationale: His 1870 message argued that government must go beyond policing and should promote public improvements and prosperity.

property-fundamental.rationale: When discussing railroad consolidation he defended the state’s continuing power of eminent domain and treated the taking of private property for public thoroughfares as legitimate.

racial-franchise.rationale: He called the possibility that Southern governments could retain voting disabilities based on race a flaw in the proposed Fourteenth Amendment.

restore-past-order.rationale: In discussing the future of the republic after the war he rejected treating earlier political orders as models to recover and placed the realization of liberty ahead of his generation.

right-to-secede.rationale: Chamberlain volunteered for the Union Army and helped defeat the Confederate forces seeking to take their states out of the United States.

separate-church-state.rationale: In the education section of his first address he called the union of church and state incompatible with American institutions.

separated-powers.rationale: In his address on the lessons of the Civil War, he endorsed checks and balances among the legislative, executive and judicial departments and warned against encroachment by one department on another.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: When addressing temperance reform he urged the legislature to work through established civil officers and warned that a special enforcement body would undermine Maine’s tradition of municipal authority.

state-directs-investment.rationale: He obtained and disbursed the Massachusetts portion of the state claims assigned to the European and North American Railroad as support for the railway’s development.

state-harmful.rationale: His 1870 message made government responsible for public safety, improvements and encouraging productive enterprises.

strong-leader.rationale: During Maine’s contested election he secured referral of the dispute to the court and turned over his temporary authority after the court resolved the conflict.

taxation-theft.rationale: He called public provision for education a duty of the state and explicitly commended the direct taxation used to support Maine’s schools.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: His centennial address linked concentrated English landownership to the loss of independent livelihoods and praised freehold tenure for freeing Maine settlers from dependence on landlords.

widespread-small-property.rationale: His centennial address blamed the displacement of small English freeholders and the concentration of their land in a few hands for widening inequality and impoverishing laborers.

notes: The four gubernatorial addresses and the centennial address were searched for public finance, industry, civil and political rights, courts, criminal justice, religion, immigration, ecology and technology. The Paris education report was checked for school finance, religious instruction, coeducation and international cooperation. The military memoir, commemorative speeches, and accounts of the 1880 transfer of power were checked for federal and state powers, elections, political means, war and Reconstruction. Chamberlain’s defense of the Union and acceptance of emancipation are documented. His description of the constitutional issue that divided the country and his account of what the war settled do not rank slavery among its underlying causes.
